# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading of the 24-Month Follow-up

This follow-up answers most of the questions left open by the earlier papers. It uses a registered follow-up protocol, adds a second hours measure (system logs) to check for unrecorded work, and pre-specifies the mediation test. It also makes a candid admission that the trial cannot separate reorganisation from the hours cut. Its arithmetic checks out:

- Output per hour, timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 ≈ +9.8%.
- Output per hour, logs: 0.966 / 0.89 ≈ +8.5%.
- Halden subset hours: 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%, and 96.8 / 86.6 ≈ +11.8%.
- The county's estimate of 12% more counter staff matches the rough calculation in my Varden reading (1 / 0.886 ≈ 1.13).

Its corrections to the two earlier papers are largely justified. Section 5 confirms that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which was the concern I raised. Several problems remain, and the most important one is not acknowledged.

## 1. The control offices were contaminated, which affects both the 24-month estimate and the decay finding

In month 15, two of the seven control case-processing offices ran a "meeting audit". Their meeting time fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour rose 4.1% against their own previous six months. The report presents this as "an unplanned observation" about whether gains can be had without cutting hours. It is also contamination of the control group, and the report doesn't discuss it in that light.

- If control output per hour rose, the gap between treated and control offices shrank. The 24-month estimate is therefore biased downward.
- A crude calculation: 2 of 7 offices × 4.1% ≈ 1.2 points on the control average for the late period. The exact effect on the 24-month estimate depends on whether it measures month 24 alone or the whole period. Either way, it could account for a meaningful share of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%.
- So part of the reported "fading" may be the control group improving, not the treatment effect decaying.
- These offices plausibly took the idea from the trial itself, since the nine-month report publicised the meetings finding. That would be a spillover from the trial, not an independent event.

The 24-month estimate should be re-run excluding the two offices, or with the post-month-15 period handled separately.

## 2. The size of the decline is overstated in places and uncertain throughout

- **The Summary compares different measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, about 22%. The body of the report makes this distinction; the Summary does not.
- **The confidence intervals overlap heavily** (6.9–18.4 against 4.6–15.2). The decline is a point estimate, not a statistically established change, and contamination may inflate it.
- **Two time points don't establish a trend.** The report rightly avoids extrapolating. It also rightly says the result is inconsistent with the gain disappearing by month ten. That rebuts Varga & Holm's extrapolation, though theirs was based on survey energy in Halden, not on output in Varden.

The fair summary is: some decline is possible and probably modest, and the gain clearly persists to 24 months.

## 3. What the log measure captures is unclear

The logs record "active log-in time on the case-management system… time staff are working on cases". The figures don't fit easily with that description.

- Timesheet hours in treated offices fell by about 4.5 hours a week (12% of 37.9). Meeting time fell by 3.5 hours (7.4 → 3.9), so time outside meetings fell by only about 1 hour.
- If logs captured only casework, log hours should have fallen by a few percent. They fell by 11%, about the same as timesheets.

Either the logs include time logged in during meetings, in which case they are not a measure of casework, or the reconciliation needs explaining. This matters because log hours are the denominator for the headline 8.5% and the outcome in the mediation model. The report should say exactly what log time includes, and report baseline log hours.

## 4. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms" suggests

- **It is partly true by definition.** If meeting hours count as hours but produce no cases, cutting them raises output per hour automatically. Removing 3.3 hours of output-free time from about 37.9 would by itself raise per-hour output by about 9.5% if output held steady. So "meetings explain 47%" is largely an accounting result. The substantive finding is that those meetings produced little output. That is still useful, but it is not evidence that the people doing the work became more efficient.
- **It is not independent of the earlier finding.** The test was registered at month 11, after the exploratory finding. It uses the same seven treated offices and, by pooling "office-months", probably some of the data already analysed. It is a pre-specified test in the same units, not a replication.
- **The effective sample size is 14 offices, not the number of office-months.** Unless the standard errors account for the clustering, intervals like 28–66% are too narrow.
- **Confounding.** Meeting cuts were not randomised. Offices with better managers may both cut meetings and improve output. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but it deserves more weight given that there are only 7 offices per arm.

The reasonable reading is that the evidence for the meetings pathway is now considerably stronger. It is not confirmed.

## 5. Issues from the nine-month report that are still open

- **Backlog and case age are still not reported.** Over 24 months with output per worker down 3.4%, whether queues are growing or deadlines are slipping is a direct test of sustainability.
- **Cost per case in the case-processing offices is not analysed.** Pay is unchanged and output per worker is down 3.4%. Overtime was claimed at nine months and may still be. So cost per case rose by at least about 3.5%. The report gives a cost figure for the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not for the arm it recommends.
- **Quality, sick days and resignations still lack confidence intervals.** The resignation figures are still a treated-versus-control comparison, not a difference-in-differences.

## 6. The Halden subset

- **Two stages of self-selection.** 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. The report frames them as survivors who continued, but non-response is a separate filter.
- **Time-tracking coverage.** Only 17 of the original 23 had time tracking (per Varga & Holm). Did all 11 continuing organisations have it? The baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to Varga & Holm's figure for 27 organisations, which is worth confirming as a recalculation for this subset rather than a reused number.
- **Reverters are excluded from the gain.** Including the three reverters, whose output was 88–91 at reversion, as an intention-to-treat style estimate would give a more honest figure for "organisations that tried it".
- **"Client-facing or coverage obligations" is stretched to fit.** The marketing agency would be classed as discretionary under the meta-analysis's coding, but it reverted over client deadlines. That suggests the discretionary/coverage-bound split is less clean than the report implies. External deadlines can behave like a coverage constraint.
- **"Upper bound" is not guaranteed.** With no comparison group, economic conditions could push the 11.8% either up or down. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate.

## 7. Minor points

- **Authors evaluating their own work.** The original Halden author co-authors the Halden follow-up, and the Varden team evaluates its own trial. Registration mitigates this but does not remove it.
- **The counter arm closed at month 12.** All long-run Varden evidence is therefore from discretionary work.
- **The "meeting audit" observation** consists of two offices, compared against their own past, over six months. It is also open to regression to the mean. The report's caution here is appropriate. A trial arm that reorganises work without cutting hours is the obvious next study.

## Where the four documents leave the question

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work, rigorous measurement | About 8–10%, persisting to 24 months. Possibly understated slightly because of control contamination. |
| Durability | Some decline from 9 to 24 months is possible, probably modest, and uncertain. The gain has not disappeared. |
| Output per worker, discretionary | Slightly below control (about −3%), so the hours cut is not fully paid for. Cost per output rises modestly. |
| Coverage-bound work | Clear loss of service with staffing fixed. Restoring service needs about 12% more staff and about 9% higher cost per contact. |
| Mechanism | A large share comes from removing low-value meeting time. This is partly an accounting effect and is not causally isolated. Fatigue contributes less. |
| Achievable without cutting hours? | Unknown. This is the most policy-relevant open question. |

The Halden headline of 23.4% roughly halves under rigorous measurement. Varga & Holm's claim that the gain is "entirely an artifact" does not hold up. The meta-analysis's claim of "no decay" was premature. What survives is a real but modest per-hour gain in discretionary work, much of it coming from removing low-value time, and a clear service loss in coverage-bound work unless staffing is increased.
